scenario.name: Play Ransomware Grixba Recon, AlphaVSS Shadow Copy Theft & Intermittent Encryption (AA23-352A)
scenario.overview: Imagine a high-ceiling logistics warehouse with towering steel pallet racks stacked with labeled shipping crates, clipboard dock stations, and a bright yellow forklift cruising down the aisle. Inside the bustling logistics warehouse, an unverified driver climbs into a parked yellow forklift and rolls toward the high-bay customer storage racks. In this real-world scenario, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the loading dock check-out clipboards in tiny disguised batches, then bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the high-bay pallet racks & forklift. The warehouse barcode inventory system flashes an urgent alert when hundreds of customer pallets are relabeled in minutes outside normal shift hours. In this scenario (T1046, Play Ransomware Grixba Recon, AlphaVSS Shadow Copy Theft & Intermittent Encryption (AA23-352A)), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: deploying Custom Grixba .NET Reconnaissance, then alphaVSS .NET Shadow Copy Mounting, then winPE APIUnhooking. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Deploying Custom Grixba .NET Reconnaissance, then AlphaVSS .NET Shadow Copy Mounting, then WinPE APIUnhooking, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: Deploying Custom Grixba .NET Reconnaissance Scanner (inf_g.exe)
stages.subtitle: Discovery & Collection (T1046 / T1560.001)
stages.description: Inside the bustling logistics warehouse, an unverified driver climbs into a parked yellow forklift and rolls toward the high-bay customer storage racks. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the loading dock check-out clipboards in tiny disguised batches while everyday visitors and the warehouse dispatcher go about their routine. Play operators staged C:\Users\Public\Music\inf_g.exe (Grixba, a custom .NET reconnaissance tool compiled with Costura.Fody to embed its DLL dependencies inside a single executable and stamped with a forged SentinelOne icon and file description) and ran inf_g.exe -m:all -d:corp.local (enumerating all Active Directory computers, WMI AntivirusProduct statuses, backup software, and active user sessions into a SQLite database compressed as ExportData.zip). Staging tools specifically inside C:\Users\Public\Music\ is a consistent operational tradecraft hallmark of Play ransomware intrusions. In the documented EventID 1 exchange from Play Ransomware Operator to Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap, Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap responds with ACK 1 (confirming that the C:\Users\Public\Music\inf_g.exe -m:all -d:corp.local request succeeded on Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap and establishing the runtime state required for Step #2 Stage 2: AlphaVSS .NET Shadow Copy Mounting for Locked Database Exfiltration). On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ C:\Users\Public\Music\inf_g.exe -m:all -d:corp.local / ⇠#1 ACK 1) from Node ① (#1 Play Ransomware Operator) to Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AlphaVSS Shadow Access & .play Shares).

stages.title: Stage 2: AlphaVSS .NET Shadow Copy Mounting for Locked Database Exfiltration
stages.subtitle: Collection & Defense Evasion (T1006 - Direct Volume Access / T1490)
stages.description: Lifting stacked pallets off the shelves, the driver slaps a brand-new shipping barcode and their own heavy padlock onto every customer crate in the bay. Here in Step 2 inside the logistics warehouse, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the loading dock check-out clipboards in tiny disguised batches without disturbing the quarantined audit cage. To steal files locked exclusively by the OS (such as C:\Windows\NTDS\ntds.dit or live SQL Server .mdf files) and subsequently wipe recovery snapshots without triggering command-line EDR rules for vssadmin.exe or wmic.exe, Play deployed a custom .NET utility loading AlphaVSS.x64.dll and AlphaFS.dll (which wrap the native Windows IVssBackupComponents COM API to create a Volume Shadow Copy, copy locked files directly from \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy*, and delete all shadow copies programmatically). Because vssadmin.exe, wmic.exe, and powershell.exe are never spawned during this step, detection rules that rely purely on process command-line strings completely miss both the ntds.dit theft and the shadow copy deletion. In the documented EventID 7 exchange from Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap to Compromised RDP / FortiOS / Exchange, Compromised RDP / FortiOS / Exchange responds with ACK 7 (confirming that the vss_copy.exe request succeeded on Compromised RDP / FortiOS / Exchange and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 Stage 3: WinPE APIUnhooking & Intermittent 0x100000-Byte Chunk Encryption (.play)). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ vss_copy.exe / ⇠#2 ACK 7) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 Compromised RDP / FortiOS / Exchange), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AlphaVSS Shadow Access & .play Shares).

stages.title: Stage 3: WinPE APIUnhooking & Intermittent 0x100000-Byte Chunk Encryption (.play)
stages.subtitle: Impact (T1486 - Data Encrypted for Impact)
stages.description: When the real warehouse dispatcher arrives for morning pickup, every pallet is locked behind someone else’s key and rerouted toward an unknown loading dock. In this final step inside the logistics warehouse, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the high-bay pallet racks & forklift until the warehouse barcode inventory log catches the mismatch. Pushed via Group Policy Objects (GPO), the Play ransomware binary dynamically resolved APIs via the Process Environment Block (PEB) to evade user-mode hooks, checked if target files already contained the 0xdeadbeef footer marker, and performed intermittent encryption (encrypting only 2, 3, or 5 specific 0x100000-byte / 1MB chunks per file depending on total file size using AES and RSA-4096, appending .play, and dropping a minimalist ReadMe.txt containing only the word "PLAY" and an email address). Encrypting only a few 1MB chunks per multi-gigabyte file reduces disk I/O by over 95%, allowing Play to corrupt terabytes of storage in minutes while keeping average file-entropy scores low enough to fool naive entropy-based ransomware detectors. In the documented EventID 11 exchange from Compromised RDP / FortiOS / Exchange to Grixba .NET Scanner (inf_g.exe), Grixba .NET Scanner (inf_g.exe) responds with ALERT 11 (confirming that the Stage 3: WinPE APIUnhooking & Intermittent 0x100000-Byte Chunk Encryption (.play) request succeeded on Grixba .NET Scanner (inf_g.exe) and completing the final execution objective of Play Ransomware Grixba Recon, AlphaVSS Shadow Copy Theft & Intermittent Encryption (AA23-352A)). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Stage 3: WinPE APIUnhooking & Intermittent 0x100000-Byte Chunk Encryption (.play) / ⇠#3 ALERT 11) from Node ③ (#3 Compromised RDP / FortiOS / Exchange) to Node ④ (#4 Grixba .NET Scanner (inf_g.exe)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 AlphaVSS Shadow Access & .play Shares).
